title: The Right Reform Rabbi | Aaron Jakes
author: https://www.nplusonemag.com/author/lisajborstgmail-com/
text: For most of my childhood, my family and I attended services at Central Synagogue, a Reform congregation in Midtown Manhattan. Every week we took our favorite spot in the Moorish Revival sanctuary, six rows back on the left, then lingered after services to schmooze with the clergy. Throughout the ’80s and ’90s, when I was attending regularly, the synagogue was an intimate but not exactly dynamic community — turnout on Friday evenings rarely exceeded a hundred people. The exception was when the congregation emerged in full force for the High Holidays, and the synagogue resorted to an undisguised class hierarchy to solve its seating problem. A “Community Service,” the most affordable option, took place in an overflow auditorium across the street. The “Family Service,” for which tickets were more costly, deviated from ritual norms by starting around sundown, forcing attendees to begin their Yom Kippur fast either early or late. Finally, the “Assigned Seating Service” occupied the main sanctuary at the appropriate times, granting proximity to the bimah on the basis of past donations. By any objective standard, everyone we knew at Central was wealthy. But on the High Holidays, it was impossible to miss the steep gradations of affluence and power.Already back then, Central’s membership included some of the country’s leading financial managers, real estate developers, and corporate executives. But the synagogue’s size and stature — its reputation as one of America’s most prominent Reform congregations — have soared since the arrival of Angela Buchdahl. Two decades ago, Buchdahl joined Central’s clergy in the role of senior cantor. She is now the synagogue’s first female head rabbi, the first Korean American rabbi ever, and the closest thing Reform Judaism has to a global superstar. Buchdahl delivers sermons that are livestreamed around the world, makes regular appearances on network morning shows to speak on matters of Jewish life, and has officiated at Jewish holiday celebrations in Washington under presidents Obama and Biden. Her New York Times–bestselling autobiography, Heart of a Stranger, recounts her meteoric rise and shattering of a rabbinical glass ceiling, making the case for a multicultural, liberal, “quintessentially American” form of Judaism. When the book was published in October 2025, Stephen Colbert was there to emcee the launch.Buchdahl was born in Seoul in 1972. Her mother, Yi Sulja, was the daughter of a Korean resistance fighter who delivered clandestine communications for the Korean independence movement during World War II; her father, Fred Warnick, was a third-generation Jewish American whose family built a successful mill-working business in Tacoma. The two met after Warnick traveled to Korea for his ROTC service requirement, and the family relocated to Tacoma when Buchdahl was 5. Growing up in the United States, Buchdahl found a sense of belonging among the local Jewish community as well as an inkling of her calling through music. Her earliest experiences of standing before a congregation came as a song leader, first at Jewish summer camps, then at home in Tacoma. “When I sang Jewish music and prayer,” Buchdahl recalls, “I came alive and felt like God heard me.” At the age of 16, she realized her dream was to become a rabbi.As the child of an interfaith and interracial marriage, Buchdahl learned early on that her efforts to gain acceptance from other Jews would be difficult and sometimes painful. Her Buddhist mother studied Hebrew, sang in the choir, and cooked “wontons for the oneg,” but she refrained from converting, and the congregation “never quite treated her as one of them.” In an early chapter, Buchdahl recalls noticing “that Mom was different from all the Jews. And that meant that I was different from all the Jews, too.” Buchdahl was 11 in 1983 when the American Reform movement broke with the halachic tradition of tracing Jewish identity through matrilineal descent alone. But in her racial and religious difference, she endured enough bruising interrogation of her status as a “real Jew” that during her senior year of college, she decided to put that skepticism to rest and formally convert.
